Clinical Reference

Asthma Exacerbation

On this page
Acute, largely reversible lower-airway obstruction — bronchospasm + airway edema + mucus plugging — that has broken through baseline control and needs a step-up in treatment. The job: reverse obstruction fast, quench inflammation early, and recognize the fatiguing patient before the PaCO₂ tells you too late.
Triad: bronchospasm · edema · mucus First-line: O₂ + SABA + systemic steroid Escalate: continuous SABA + ipratropium + IV Mg²⁺ "Normal" PaCO₂ in a tiring asthmatic = pre-arrest Silent chest = life-threatening
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story

Asthma is a chronic Type-2 (Th2) inflammatory airway disease. In most patients an inhaled trigger (virus, allergen, smoke, cold air, exercise, aspirin/NSAID) is presented by dendritic cells to Th2 lymphocytes, which release IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13. IL-4/IL-13 drive B-cells to class-switch to IgE and push goblet-cell mucus metaplasia; IL-5 recruits and activates eosinophils. IgE coats mast cells — on re-exposure they degranulate, releasing histamine, prostaglandins and leukotrienes. That produces an early phase (bronchospasm within minutes) followed 6–12 h later by a late phase of eosinophilic infiltration and airway wall edema.

An exacerbation is that inflammation acutely tipping three mechanical problems past a threshold:

  1. Bronchospasm — airway smooth-muscle constriction (seconds–minutes; the reversible part a bronchodilator fixes).
  2. Airway-wall edema & inflammation — takes hours–days and only a steroid truly reverses.
  3. Mucus plugging — hypertrophied goblet cells and mucous glands fill the small airways with tenacious plugs (Curschmann spirals).

All three narrow the airway. Because airways narrow more on exhalation, gas gets trapped → dynamic hyperinflation and auto-PEEP (intrinsic PEEP), a flattened diaphragm, and a steep rise in the work of breathing. Heterogeneous obstruction creates V/Q mismatch → hypoxemia, and the huge inspiratory effort against closed airways produces a large pulsus paradoxus; in the extreme, hyperinflation chokes venous return → obstructive shock.

Breathing through an asthmatic airway is like breathing through a wet, half-collapsed paper straw. The bronchodilator pops the straw a little wider (muscle), but the straw is also soggy and clogged (edema + mucus) — only the steroid dries and unclogs it over hours. If you keep forcing air in faster than it can escape, the straw balloons and traps air (auto-PEEP) until almost nothing moves — the silent chest.
Exacerbation cascade — trigger → Type-2 inflammation → the three mechanical obstructions → air trapping/auto-PEEP → fatigue → hypercapnic failure. Dashed arrows show where each drug class interrupts the chain.
Asthmatic airway: smooth-muscle hypertrophy, sub-epithelial fibrosis, and luminal mucus — the structural substrate of obstruction.
Image: Hsieh, A., Assadinia, N., &amp; Hackett, T. — CC BY 4.0. Wikimedia Commons
Curschmann spiral — a cast of coiled mucus shed from a plugged small airway, classically seen in asthmatic sputum.
Image: From one of the pathogists at work. — Attribution. Wikimedia Commons
Every therapy in this guide maps to one step in that cascade: SABA (albuterol) → β₂-receptor → relaxes constricted smooth muscle; SAMA (ipratropium) → blocks M3 muscarinic tone → extra bronchodilation + less secretion; systemic corticosteroids → genomic suppression of the eosinophilic/IL-driven inflammation → reverse edema and prevent relapse (they take ~4–6 h to bite, so give early); IV magnesium → blocks calcium influx into smooth muscle → bronchodilation in the sickest; oxygen → corrects V/Q-mismatch hypoxemia. Understand the straw and every drug order writes itself.
🩸

The ABG story — the sequence that predicts the crash

Blood-gas evolution in a worsening attack is a countdown clock. Memorize the order — the deceptive middle step kills people:

StageABG patternWhat it means
1 · Early / mild–moderate↓PaCO₂, ↑pH (respiratory alkalosis), normal PaO₂Hyperventilating and compensating well. Expected and reassuring.
2 · Worsening (the trap)"Normal" PaCO₂ (35–45 mmHg), pH normalizing, ↓PaO₂A tachypneic asthmatic should be hypocapnic. A "normal" CO₂ means the respiratory muscles are tiring — an ominous, not reassuring, number.
3 · Impending failure↑PaCO₂, ↓pH (respiratory acidosis), hypoxemiaVentilatory failure. Prepare for ICU / intubation; do not chase a single number — treat the patient.
A normalizing or rising PaCO₂ with a silent chest, exhaustion, or altered mental status defines life-threatening / near-fatal asthma. This is the moment to call ICU and get airway help at the bedside — not to order another neb and wait.
📊

Severity classification — GINA 2025 & BTS/SIGN side by side

Two guideline systems, slightly different cut-points. Both are presented rather than merged — use whichever your institution follows, and always err toward the higher tier.

GINA 2025 — ED / acute-care assessment (adults ≥12 y)

FeatureMild–ModerateSevereLife-threatening
SpeechPhrases; prefers sittingWords; hunched forward—
AgitationNot agitatedAgitatedDrowsy / confused
Respiratory rateIncreased>30/min—
Accessory musclesNot usedIn use—
Pulse100–120 bpm>120 bpmBradycardia (pre-arrest)
SpO₂ (room air)90–95%<90%<90%
PEF>50% pred/best≤50% pred/bestUnable / <33%
ChestWheezeLoud wheezeSilent chest

Source: GINA 2025 Global Strategy (ginasthma.org). GINA groups mild + moderate for management; the practical escalate trigger is PEF ≤50%, SpO₂ <90%, or inability to speak in phrases.

BTS/SIGN/NICE (SIGN 158/244) — UK severity bands, adults

CategoryDefining criteria (any one qualifies for the higher tier)
ModeratePEF >50–75% best/predicted; SpO₂ ≥92%; speech normal; RR <25; HR <110.
Acute severePEF 33–50%; cannot complete a sentence in one breath; RR ≥25/min; HR ≥110/min.
Life-threateningPEF <33%; SpO₂ <92%; PaO₂ <60 mmHg; "normal" PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg; silent chest, cyanosis, poor effort; arrhythmia; hypotension; exhaustion; altered consciousness.
Near-fatalRaised PaCO₂ and/or requiring mechanical ventilation with raised inflation pressures.

Source: BTS/SIGN/NICE acute asthma pathway (SIGN 158/244). NAEPP EPR-3 uses FEV₁/PEF >40% (mild-moderate), <40% (severe), <25% (impending arrest).

Wheeze loudness does not track severity — the loudest wheeze can be the least sick, and the silent chest is the most sick. Trust objective PEF/FEV₁ and SpO₂ over the stethoscope's volume.

Presentation & findings — and why

🩺

Symptoms & signs — frequency and the mechanism behind each

Read each finding as evidence of one of the three obstructions or of the compensations they trigger. Frequencies are approximate for adults presenting acutely.

Finding~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
Dyspnea / breathlessness~95%Airflow limitation + air trapping raise the work of breathing; the defining symptom of an attack.
Wheeze (expiratory)~80–90%Turbulent flow through narrowed intrathoracic airways; worst on exhalation when airways narrow further. Absent = too little airflow (silent chest) or no obstruction.
Cough (often nocturnal)~75%Airway irritant-receptor stimulation + mucus; frequently the earliest and last symptom of a flare.
Chest tightness~65%Bronchoconstriction + hyperinflation stretch airway/chest-wall mechanoreceptors.
Tachypnea (↑RR)~60%Hypoxemia + hypercapnia + J-receptor drive; RR ≥25 (BTS) / >30 (GINA severe) is a severity marker.
Tachycardia (HR >110–120)~55%Sympathetic drive, hypoxemia, and β-agonist effect; a falling HR with worsening distress is pre-arrest.
Accessory-muscle use / tripoding~30–40%Recruitment of sternocleidomastoid/scalenes when the flattened diaphragm can't cope — a severe sign.
Inability to speak full sentences~25–35%Breathlessness interrupts speech; "words only" = severe, per GINA/BTS.
Pulsus paradoxus >10–12 mmHg<15%Large negative intrathoracic pressure swings + hyperinflation exaggerate the normal inspiratory BP fall; correlates with severity.
Silent chest / cyanosis / drowsiness<10%Airflow too low to make a sound + failing gas exchange — life-threatening, intubation territory.
Read the patternSpeech, RR, HR, SpO₂ and PEF are your five bedside dials. Two or more in the "severe" column, or any life-threatening feature, buys continuous bronchodilator + IV steroid + magnesium and a call to critical care.
🪛

Imaging & objective findings — when they appear

Asthma is a clinical + spirometric diagnosis — imaging is to exclude mimics/complications, not to confirm the attack.

FindingWhen / thresholdWhy
PEF / FEV₁ reduced (% personal best or predicted)At presentation — alwaysDirectly quantifies airflow limitation; the single most useful severity measure. Repeat after treatment to gauge response.
SpO₂ <92% (BTS) / <90% (GINA)Severe/life-threatening flagV/Q mismatch outpaces compensation; triggers an ABG and controlled O₂.
CXR: pulmonary hyperinflation (flat diaphragms, ↑retrosternal air, >9 posterior ribs)If CXR obtainedAir trapping/dynamic hyperinflation; supports severity but not routinely needed.
CXR: pneumothorax / pneumomediastinumSudden deterioration, chest pain, asymmetryBarotrauma from high airway pressures/air trapping — an emergency; get a CXR.
CXR: focal consolidationFever, purulent sputum, focal signsPneumonia as the trigger — the only common reason antibiotics enter the picture.
Order a CXR only for suspected pneumothorax, pneumonia, life-threatening asthma, or failure to respond — not on every wheezer. Never delay bronchodilator + oxygen for a film.
Hyperinflated lungs: flattened diaphragms and increased lung volume from air trapping — the radiographic signature of severe obstruction.

🧪

Reading the labs — what each value is telling you

LabWhat it means & why it moves
ABG — PaCO₂The most important number in a sick asthmatic. Early it is low (hyperventilation). A normal or rising PaCO₂ in a distressed patient signals respiratory-muscle fatigue → impending failure, not improvement. Do not be falsely reassured by a "normal" gas.
ABG — pHHigh early (respiratory alkalosis) → normalizes → then falls (respiratory acidosis of ventilatory failure). A superimposed lactic (metabolic) acidosis from work of breathing and high-dose β-agonist can co-exist.
PaO₂ / SpO₂Falls with V/Q mismatch. SpO₂ <92% (BTS) prompts an ABG. Profound hypoxemia despite high-flow O₂ = severe shunt/mucus plugging.
PotassiumFalls with high-dose β₂-agonists (drive K⁺ intracellularly) and steroids — watch for hypokalemia and arrhythmia during continuous nebs; replace and monitor.
LactateRises from respiratory-muscle anaerobic work and as a direct β-agonist effect (type B lactic acidosis) — a high lactate here is often benign pharmacology, not sepsis; interpret with the clinical picture.
GlucoseRises with β-agonists and systemic corticosteroids — expect and monitor, especially in diabetics.
Blood eosinophils / FeNONot for acute triage; useful later to characterize Type-2-high phenotype and select biologics/ICS intensity in refractory or severe asthma.
CBC / CRPNeutrophilia can be steroid- or stress-driven, not infection. Only pursue antibiotics if a bacterial trigger (pneumonia) is genuinely present.
Peak-flow meter — bedside PEF as % of personal best is the fastest objective severity and response measure.

🩺 Clinic — outpatient control, the exacerbation action plan & prevention
Assess

Recognizing a flare in clinic

🔍

How it presents & who is high-risk

Increasing use of reliever inhaler, night waking with cough/wheeze, dropping PEF on a home diary, or reduced exercise tolerance are the early markers of a flare — often over days. Ask specifically about reliever canister use and prior severe attacks.

Risk factors for asthma-related death (GINA 2025) — any one lowers your threshold to treat aggressively and escalate: prior near-fatal attack requiring intubation; asthma admission or ED visit in the last 12 months; currently/recently on oral steroids; not on ICS or poor adherence/technique; SABA over-use (≥1 canister/month, or ≥12/year); food allergy with asthma; psychiatric/psychosocial problems; no written action plan.

Chronic control — the GINA step ladder

💊

Prevent the next flare: first-line → escalation (GINA 2025)

GINA 2025 offers two tracks. Track 1 (preferred) uses ICS-formoterol as the reliever at every step (AIR = anti-inflammatory reliever; MART = maintenance-and-reliever therapy) — this reduces severe exacerbations vs a SABA reliever because every rescue puff also delivers a steroid. Track 2 keeps a SABA reliever with separate ICS/ICS-LABA controller — used when Track 1 isn't feasible or preferred.

The single most important step-change in modern asthma care: SABA-only treatment is out. Because the exacerbation is inflammatory, giving a steroid with every reliever (ICS-formoterol) treats the cause each time the patient reaches for rescue — cutting severe attacks (SYGMA, Novel START).

Monitor

Follow-up & the action plan

📈

What to recheck, and when

  • After any exacerbation: review within 2 working days (primary care) and in a respiratory clinic within 4 weeks (BTS/SIGN).
  • Every visit: assess control (symptom frequency, night waking, reliever use, activity limitation), inhaler technique, adherence, and trigger exposure; check PEF/spirometry.
  • Written asthma action plan with personalized PEF zones (green >80%, yellow 50–80%, red <50% of best) — proven to reduce hospitalizations.
  • Step down only after ≥3 months of good control; reducing ICS by ~25–50% at a time.
Comorbidities

How comorbidities change asthma

🔗

Interactions & what changes in management

ComorbidityHow it interactsWhat changes
Allergic rhinitis / chronic rhinosinusitis + nasal polypsShared Type-2 inflammation ("one airway"); untreated upper-airway disease worsens control.Treat with intranasal steroids; polyps + asthma + aspirin sensitivity = AERD — avoid NSAIDs, consider dupilumab.
GERDMicro-aspiration & vagal reflex trigger cough/bronchospasm; often silent.Treat symptomatic reflux (PPI); empiric PPI for asymptomatic GERD does not improve asthma.
ObesityRestrictive mechanics + systemic inflammation; often steroid-resistant, poorer control.Weight loss improves control; consider OSA screening; expect less ICS responsiveness.
Obstructive sleep apneaNocturnal symptoms, worse control, harder-to-treat asthma.Screen and treat with CPAP — improves asthma control.
ABPA (aspergillus hypersensitivity)Recurrent flares, ↑↑IgE, central bronchiectasis, fleeting infiltrates.Systemic steroids ± antifungal (itraconazole); suspect in steroid-dependent asthma.
Cardiac disease / HFpEF"Cardiac asthma" mimics wheeze; β-agonists ↑HR/arrhythmia; theophylline pro-arrhythmic.Distinguish with BNP/echo; use β-agonists cautiously; avoid non-selective β-blockers (see below).
Pregnancy~1/3 worsen; hypoxemia harms the fetus more than the medications do.Keep treating — ICS (budesonide best-studied), SABA, and systemic steroids are all used; under-treatment is the real danger.
Drugs to avoid / use with caution in asthma
  • Non-selective β-blockers (propranolol, timolol eye drops, carvedilol, nadolol) — block β₂ → bronchospasm; can be fatal. If a β-blocker is essential (e.g., post-MI), use a cardioselective agent (metoprolol, bisoprolol) cautiously.
  • Aspirin & NSAIDs — trigger bronchospasm in AERD (aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, ~7% of asthmatics); use acetaminophen/leukotriene modifiers instead.
  • Sedatives / opioids / benzodiazepines — suppress respiratory drive; never sedate a distressed asthmatic without controlling the airway.
  • Excessive / uncontrolled high-flow oxygen — can worsen V/Q matching and mask deterioration; titrate to SpO₂ 93–95% (GINA) / 94–98% (BTS), not 100%.
  • Cholinergic agents / adenosine / certain contrast — can provoke bronchospasm.

Prevent

USPSTF A/B, vaccines & prevention

🛡️

Grade A & B recommendations relevant to asthma patients

The USPSTF does not screen for asthma itself, but these Grade A/B recommendations are high-yield for this population (many asthma flares are triggered by tobacco smoke and respiratory infections):

GradeRecommendationPopulation
AAsk about tobacco use & provide cessation interventions (behavioral + pharmacotherapy)All adults; smoking is a major asthma trigger & accelerates decline
ACounsel to prevent tobacco use / offer interventionsSchool-age children & adolescents
BScreen for unhealthy alcohol use & brief counselingAdults ≥18 y
BScreen for depression / anxietyAdults & adolescents (psychosocial burden ↑ asthma risk)
BScreen for obesity & offer/refer to behavioral interventionAdults with BMI ≥30 (obesity worsens control)

Immunizations (ACIP — not USPSTF, but essential): annual influenza vaccine; pneumococcal vaccination (asthma on chronic steroids/severe disease is an indication); COVID-19 per schedule; consider RSV per current age/risk criteria. Reducing viral triggers prevents exacerbations.

Escalate

When to send to the ED / admit

🚑

Red flags → don't manage this in clinic

Send to the ED / call EMS for any of: PEF <50% best (or <33% = life-threatening), SpO₂ <94% on room air, words-only speech, RR ≥25 / HR ≥110, accessory-muscle use, poor response to reliever, exhaustion, or any prior near-fatal attack. Give SABA + oral steroid + controlled O₂ while arranging transfer — do not wait.
🛏️ Wards — acute inpatient management
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria & risk profile

Admit if, after 1 hour of intensive treatment, any of the following persist: PEF <50–75% best/predicted with ongoing symptoms, SpO₂ <94%, incomplete/absent response to bronchodilator, or any risk factor for fatal asthma. Merck: admit if no improvement by 4 hours.

Straight to ICU/HDU for any life-threatening or near-fatal feature at presentation (silent chest, SpO₂ <92%, normal/rising PaCO₂, exhaustion, altered mental status).

Severity-driven triage: initial band → therapy intensity → reassess at 1 h → discharge vs escalate.

Acute management — the ladder

💊

First-line → escalation, with doses (GINA / BTS / EPR-3)

Sequence maps to the cascade: oxygen corrects hypoxemia; SABA relaxes muscle immediately; ipratropium adds muscarinic bronchodilation; systemic steroid reverses the inflammation/edema (give within the first hour); IV magnesium is the smooth-muscle rescue for those not responding.

Monitor

What to trend each day

📈

Daily assessment targets

  • PEF pre- & post-bronchodilator (aim for a rising trend toward >75% best) and diurnal variability.
  • SpO₂ / oxygen requirement — weaning O₂ is a marker of recovery.
  • Work of breathing / RR / speech — the bedside gestalt; accessory-muscle use should resolve.
  • Reliever frequency — spacing out of nebs/puffs signals readiness to step down.
  • Potassium & glucose during continuous β-agonist + steroids; replace K⁺, cover glucose.
  • Inhaler technique teaching — start before discharge, not on the day of.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Floor → ICU triggers (BTS/SIGN)

Transfer to ICU/HDU for any of: deteriorating PEF; persisting/worsening hypoxia (SpO₂ <92%, PaO₂ <60 mmHg); hypercapnia / normal or rising PaCO₂; falling pH / rising H⁺ on ABG; exhaustion, feeble respiration; drowsiness / confusion / coma; silent chest, cyanosis; hemodynamic instability; or respiratory arrest. Get airway/critical-care help before the crash.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness (BTS/SIGN & GINA): PEF >75% best/predicted with diurnal variability <25%; SpO₂ ≥94% on room air; reliever use spaced to ≥4-hourly and stable off nebs for ≥24 h; symptoms controlled; safe inhaler technique demonstrated.

The discharge bundle — never skip:

  • Complete oral steroid course (≥5 days total).
  • Start/continue ICS-containing controller — never discharge on SABA alone (GINA 2025).
  • Check & correct inhaler technique and adherence.
  • Provide/update a written asthma action plan with PEF zones.
  • Primary-care review within 2 working days; respiratory clinic within 4 weeks.
  • Address triggers & modifiable risk factors (smoking, adherence, allergen exposure).

Home

Most patients — PEF >75%, stable, self-manages with an action plan.

Home health

Frail/elderly needing nursing check-ins, inhaler-technique reinforcement, or O₂ setup.

SNF

Deconditioned or with comorbidities needing skilled nursing <3 h therapy/day before home.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Rare — prolonged critical illness/ICU deconditioning tolerating ≥3 h therapy/day.

LTAC

Prolonged vent weaning after near-fatal asthma requiring extended mechanical support.

Palliative

Rarely relevant; consider for end-stage overlapping COPD or irreversible respiratory failure with goals-of-care shift.
🫀 ICU — near-fatal asthma & ventilatory support
Admit

ICU triggers

🚨

When it belongs in the unit

ICU/HDU for life-threatening or near-fatal features, or poor response to intensive ward therapy:

  • Silent chest, cyanosis, or feeble respiratory effort
  • Exhaustion, drowsiness, confusion, or coma
  • SpO₂ <92% / PaO₂ <60 mmHg despite high-flow O₂
  • Normal or rising PaCO₂, falling pH / rising H⁺ (ventilatory failure)
  • Deteriorating PEF despite maximal therapy
  • Hemodynamic instability / arrhythmia; respiratory or cardiac arrest
Near-fatal asthma = raised PaCO₂ and/or needing mechanical ventilation with high inflation pressures. Have the most experienced airway operator, drugs, and a plan for post-intubation hyperinflation ready before you tube.
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Continuous SpO₂ + capnography; serial ABGs (trend PaCO₂ and pH, not a single value).
  • Arterial line for frequent ABGs & beat-to-beat BP (large pulsus paradoxus).
  • Cardiac monitoring — continuous β-agonist + hypokalemia + hypoxemia are arrhythmogenic; follow K⁺, Mg²⁺, glucose, lactate.
  • If ventilated: monitor auto-PEEP, plateau pressure, and expiratory flow for breath-stacking.
  • Central access if on multiple infusions/vasopressors; watch for barotrauma (serial exam ± CXR).
Support

Critical-care pharmacotherapy

💉

Maximal medical therapy & rescue agents — mechanism, dose, when

AgentMechanismDoseRoleWhen to pick
Albuterol (continuous neb)β₂-agonist → smooth-muscle relaxation10–15 mg/h continuous, O₂-drivenBackbone bronchodilatorAll severe/life-threatening
IpratropiumM3 muscarinic antagonist0.5 mg neb q4–6 h (front-loaded q20min ×3)Additive bronchodilationAdd to SABA in severe
Magnesium sulfateBlocks Ca²⁺ influx → smooth-muscle relaxation1.2–2 g IV over 20 min (± infusion in refractory)Rescue bronchodilatorPoor response to inhaled therapy
Systemic corticosteroidGenomic anti-inflammatoryMethylprednisolone 60–80 mg/day IV (or hydrocortisone 100 mg q6h)Reverses inflammationAll — continue through ICU stay
KetamineNMDA antagonist; catecholamine release → bronchodilationInduction 1–2 mg/kg IV; infusion 0.5–1 mg/kg/hInduction + bronchodilator sedationIntubation of the asthmatic; refractory bronchospasm
Epinephrine (IM/SC)α+β agonist0.3–0.5 mg IM (1 mg/mL) q5–10 minAnaphylaxis / near-arrest rescueAnaphylactic trigger or peri-arrest when inhaled route failing
Terbutaline (SC/IV)β₂-agonist (parenteral)0.25 mg SC; IV per protocolSystemic β-agonistInhaled delivery inadequate (poor air entry)
Aminophylline IVNon-selective PDE inhibitorSpecialist, level-guidedLast-line adjunctRarely — near-fatal, no response; not routine
Note the theme: these are bronchodilators + anti-inflammatories, not pressors. True vasopressors (norepinephrine) are only needed for the obstructive/peri-intubation shock that hyperinflation causes — treat the cause (reduce ventilation, allow exhalation) rather than chasing the BP with pressors alone.
Airway

NIV, intubation & the ventilator

🌬️

Controlled hypoventilation / permissive hypercapnia

NIV may be trialed early in a monitored setting (RR >25, accessory-muscle use, PaCO₂ 40–60 mmHg), but the evidence is weaker than in COPD — do not let it delay intubation in a failing patient.

Intubation is a clinical decision: cardiac/respiratory arrest, imminent arrest despite maximal therapy, declining mental status, PaCO₂ >60 mmHg with worsening acidosis, refractory hypoxemia, or exhaustion. Induce with ketamine 1–2 mg/kg (sedative + bronchodilator); paralyze with rocuronium/vecuronium (low histamine release). Use the largest-bore ETT available to reduce resistance and ease suctioning.

The peri-intubation period is the danger zone: sedation + positive pressure on an already hyperinflated chest can collapse venous return → obstructive shock / PEA arrest. Give fluids, have push-dose epinephrine/vasopressor ready, and if the patient crashes on the vent, disconnect the circuit and press on the chest to allow full exhalation — and exclude tension pneumothorax.

Initial ventilator settings — minimize dynamic hyperinflation

Mode
Volume A/C
volume-cycled assist-control
Tidal volume
5–8 mL/kg
IBW; aim ~6 mL/kg
Resp. rate
10–12/min

Insp. flow
>80–100 L/min

I:E ratio

PEEP

pH target
7.20–7.25
permissive hypercapnia; tolerate ↑PaCO₂
The enemy is breath-stacking / auto-PEEP: if you don't give the obstructed lung enough time to exhale, pressure and volume climb until barotrauma or arrest. Every setting above is engineered to lengthen expiration and lower minute ventilation — accept a high CO₂ (permissive hypercapnia) as long as oxygenation is adequate and pH ≥7.20. Give bicarbonate only for severe acidemia.
Rescue

Advanced / rescue therapies

⚙️

When maximal ventilation isn't enough

  • Ketamine infusion — 0.5–1 mg/kg/h for ongoing bronchodilator sedation.
  • Inhalational anesthetics (sevoflurane/isoflurane) — potent bronchodilators for refractory bronchospasm in the OR/ICU.
  • Heliox (70:30 or 80:20 He:O₂) — lower gas density improves laminar flow through obstructed airways; a temporizing bridge (limited by FiO₂ ceiling).
  • Deep sedation ± neuromuscular blockade — to abolish patient–ventilator dyssynchrony and reduce O₂ consumption (limit paralysis duration — steroid + paralytic myopathy risk).
  • ECMO (veno-venous) — rescue for refractory near-fatal asthma with life-threatening hypercapnia/hypoxemia despite optimal ventilation; excellent outcomes reported in this reversible disease.
  • Bronchoscopy / mucolytics — occasionally for lobar collapse from mucus plugging (evidence limited).
Asthma is reversible — the airways will open with time and anti-inflammatory therapy. Rescue devices (ECMO) exist to buy that time; a young status-asthmaticus patient is exactly who deserves aggressive rescue support.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Downgrade when: extubated and maintaining SpO₂ ≥94% on low-flow O₂/room air; PaCO₂ & pH normalized off aggressive support; PEF trending >50% and rising; reliever spaced to ≥q2–4 h; off continuous nebulization and IV magnesium; hemodynamically stable; alert.
Not yet if: still requiring continuous SABA, high O₂ needs, borderline gas exchange, persistent accessory-muscle use, or within hours of extubation with unproven airway stability.

Guidelines

  • GINA 2025 — Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention: Full report · Summary guide (Track 1/2, AIR/MART, O₂ 93–95%, severity table, risk factors for death).
  • BTS/SIGN/NICE — acute asthma in adults (SIGN 158/244): Hospital pathway · General practice (severity bands, O₂ 94–98%, ipratropium 0.5 mg, magnesium 1.2–2 g, discharge PEF >75%).
  • NAEPP Expert Panel Report 3 (EPR-3), Section 5 — Managing Exacerbations (NHLBI): ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK7228 (+ 2020 Focused Updates: SMART, LAMA, FeNO).
  • Merck Manual Professional — Treatment of Acute Asthma Exacerbations: merckmanuals.com (dosing, NIV/intubation thresholds, permissive hypercapnia).
  • StatPearls — Status Asthmaticus: ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK526070. AMBOSS — Acute asthma exacerbation: amboss.com.
  • Mechanical ventilation in severe asthma — Critical Care review: ccforum.biomedcentral.com · Deranged Physiology: Ventilation strategies for status asthmaticus. ECMO rescue: PMC8720297.
  • USPSTF — Tobacco cessation (Grade A), alcohol/depression/obesity screening (Grade B): Recommendation topics.

💡

Practice-changing pearls

  1. A "normal" PaCO₂ in a distressed, tachypneic asthmatic signals fatigue → impending failure, not improvement.
  2. Silent chest = too little airflow to wheeze = life-threatening; act, don't wait.
  3. Never discharge on SABA alone (GINA 2025) — always ICS-containing therapy; SABA-only increases exacerbations and death.
  4. SABA over-use ≥12 canisters/year is a marker of death risk — count the canisters.
  5. Wheeze loudness does not track severity — trust objective PEF/FEV₁ and SpO₂.
  6. Give systemic steroids early (within the hour); they take ~4–6 h to act.
  7. Target SpO₂ 93–95% (GINA) — not 100%; over-oxygenation can worsen outcomes.
  8. Antibiotics are not routine — most triggers are viral.
  9. Non-selective β-blockers can be fatal; cardioselective only if essential.
  10. In AERD, aspirin/NSAIDs trigger bronchospasm — use acetaminophen/leukotriene modifiers.
  11. After intubation the enemy is dynamic hyperinflation/auto-PEEP — long expiratory time, low minute ventilation, permissive hypercapnia (pH ≥7.20).
  12. If a ventilated asthmatic suddenly crashes: disconnect the circuit to allow full exhalation and rule out tension pneumothorax.
  13. Ketamine is the induction agent of choice (bronchodilator + sedative).
  14. Keep treating asthma in pregnancy — hypoxemia harms the fetus far more than the medications.
